name: Growth hormone peptides at bedtime

lead: Some users take growth hormone secretagogue peptides, such as ipamorelin and CJC-1295, shortly before bed to add to the natural growth hormone pulse during sleep. The payoff they want is better recovery and repair, a leaner and more muscular look and better skin quality.

These peptides act on the ghrelin receptor (ipamorelin) or the GHRH receptor (CJC-1295) to stimulate pituitary GH release, and many also raise IGF-1. Practitioners say bedtime timing lines the dose up with the body's own nocturnal release. The drug class is mainly studied and approved for growth hormone deficiency; no published trial has tested the bedtime practice in people without a deficiency.

paras: Users administer these peptides by injection in the evening, typically as a recurring routine over weeks, often alongside training and sleep optimization. Results are usually described as gradual body composition and recovery changes.

These compounds are not approved for cosmetic use. Many secretagogues also raise prolactin and cortisol. Products sold as research chemicals are unregulated, and no safety data exist for the bedtime practice.

angle.text: Users take GH-releasing peptides such as ipamorelin and CJC-1295 before bed to amplify the sleep-time GH pulse, aiming for better recovery, a leaner, more muscular look and better skin. The peptides are studied for growth hormone deficiency.

lead: Growth hormone peptides at bedtime is a practice in which people use growth hormone secretagogues, such as ipamorelin, CJC-1295 or sermorelin, shortly before sleep. The goal is to add to the pulse of growth hormone (GH) that the body releases during early deep sleep, with the aim of supporting recovery, leaner body composition and a more youthful look.[1][2]

The appearance chain proponents describe runs through GH and IGF-1: more GH at night means more IGF-1, which is linked to muscle growth, fat breakdown and tissue repair, so training recovers faster and body composition shifts toward more muscle and less fat. Some also expect better skin and sleep quality. In forum discussion the practice is mostly framed around sermorelin and related peptides, and is sometimes paired with advice to get IGF-1 measured by blood test first.[3][4]

Growth hormone secretagogues are a recognised drug class that stimulate GH secretion by acting on the ghrelin receptor (for example ipamorelin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6 and ibutamoren) or on the GHRH receptor (for example CJC-1295, sermorelin and tesamorelin).[1] Their main clinical use is treating growth hormone deficiency.[1] No published trial has tested the bedtime practice, or appearance outcomes from it, in people without a deficiency.
infobox: Largest daily GH pulse about an hour after sleep onset [2]
Unapproved for cosmetic or anti-aging use

paras: The practice combines a class of peptides with a timing rationale. Proponents reason that GH secretion is highest during early sleep and that a secretagogue taken beforehand adds to it.[3] This timing rationale comes mainly from community discussion and not from trials of these peptides.

Different community posts describe the practice with different peptides. Sermorelin posts discuss bedtime timing and its use as a monotherapy in younger people with pituitary reserve; other posts describe stacking ipamorelin with CJC-1295.[3][4]

GH is released from the anterior pituitary in pulses controlled mainly by hypothalamic GHRH and somatostatin. The largest predictable peak comes about an hour after sleep onset, nearly half of daily GH release occurs during the deepest non-REM stages, and sleep deprivation generally suppresses release, especially after early adulthood.[2] Adolescents secrete about 700 micrograms per day and healthy adults about 400.[2]

GH is anabolic: it promotes lipolysis, increases protein synthesis and supports bone mineralization. In adults with deficiency, fat mass rises and muscle mass falls, and replacement therapy is associated with reduced fat and increased lean mass.[2] A 2007 meta-analysis of healthy elderly people given GH reported about 2 kg more muscle and 2 kg less fat without a strength gain.[2]

Secretagogues act on two receptors: the ghrelin or growth hormone secretagogue receptor and the GHRH receptor. Many also raise IGF-1 and other pituitary and hypothalamic hormones, including prolactin and cortisol.[1] Wikipedia lists CJC-1295 as a long-acting GHRH analogue for which a 2006 study reported prolonged GH and IGF-1 stimulation in healthy adults, and tesamorelin as a GHRH analogue studied in HIV-associated lipodystrophy.[1]

The International Olympic Committee and the NCAA ban GH, and WADA introduced blood tests that can distinguish natural from recombinant GH around the 2004 Athens Olympics.[2] In the US, a 1990 federal law made distribution of human GH for non-authorized uses a felony, and the DEA in 2015 published a position treating off-label HGH prescription as illegal; Wikipedia notes that GH's efficacy and safety for anti-aging has not been tested in a clinical trial.[2] Secretagogues sold online as research chemicals are not approved for cosmetic use.

No studies found on bedtime use of these peptides for appearance outcomes. Registered trials involving growth hormone address other settings, such as a 16-person early-phase trial of low-dose GH on insulin sensitivity and cortisol production in GH deficiency, a 44-person phase 3 trial of a long-acting GH (MOD-4023) in children with deficiency, and a 98-child phase 3 trial of GH in children born small for gestational age.[5][6][7] One terminated 8-person trial examined gabapentin and hormone release during sleep in older men.[8]
Many secretagogues raise prolactin and cortisol, and GH itself induces insulin resistance and reduces liver glucose uptake.[1][2] No safety data exist for the bedtime practice itself.

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar forums, GH-releasing peptides are discussed as an alternative to injectable GH, with bedtime timing a frequent topic.[3][4]
